item.title: Why parents love a school with bogus numbers
item.description: Alpha School’s growth scores aren’t real. Alpha School’s growth is.
item.content:encoded:
By Kelsey Piper

Alpha School — a franchise of private schools advertising their ability to teach students more than traditional schools in vastly less time — are cropping up all over the country. There’s one in my neighborhood, and there’s another across the bay in San Francisco that charges $75,000 a year. Austin has a bunch of them, including the Texas Sports Academy — whose pitch seems to be that you can get your education out of the way as fast as possible so you can spend more time on athletics — NextGen Academy for gamers, Founders School for entrepreneurs, and Montessorium, which blends the Alpha model with Montessori teachings.

The commonality among all Alpha schools is the company’s “2 Hour Learning” technology, called Timeback. The idea is that every day, each student gets assigned two hours of activities to complete through a variety of edtech apps. These can include passages with reading comprehension questions, math lessons and practice problems, and recording apps to help students practice public speaking.

The work is individualized to the student’s current learning level. They’re supposed to get through their work as quickly as possible to free up the rest of the day for programs and workshops. And the company claims that, as a result, the kids learn much more quickly than kids at normal schools.

Share

One of Alpha’s innovations is that the kids themselves are highly successful marketers for the program — alumni write articles about Alpha’s merits, and I see children constantly in short-form videos, showing off their checklists of skills to master before they move on to the next grade.

Alpha is quite specific about just how much faster its students learn. If you go to the website of Alpha Anywhere, the company’s homeschool/remote learning platform, it will tell you it offers “mastery-based learning tailored to your child, built for 2x faster learning in 2 hours a day, from anywhere.” If you look for their gifted and talented program, that one advertises “3-7x faster learning.”

As an education reporter, one of the questions I’ve been asked the most often over the past year is, “Is that true?” If it were, the implications would be incredible. A student who masters twice as much material in a year in math, for example, could take calculus in sixth grade.

But the numbers don’t mean that. They actually don’t mean much at all.

The headline claims of “2x growth” come from numbers that have been massaged to the point of being useless for understanding what kids are learning. And insofar as there’s a secret sauce to Alpha School — and there’s definitely something — it is decidedly not the collection of edtech apps that they package as Timeback. I’ve tested those out and suspect whatever makes Alpha tick cannot be found in those apps.

The Alpha School franchise has been growing despite repeated scrutiny in the press. As I tried to understand their test scores and student outcomes, it became clear to me that a lot of parents understood perfectly well that Alpha’s marketing was overstating the company’s case — and they loved their kids’ Alpha schools all the same.

Alpha’s appeal seems to lie not so much in the “2x growth” on the webpage but instead in the particular location it has staked in the culture wars over the purpose of education — and the eternal appeal of selecting a rich, tech-savvy, ambitious peer group for your kids.

What 2x learning means

Alpha says that its students show “2x growth” if they meet certain criteria on an adaptive standardized test called MAP Growth. Alpha projects each student’s expected growth in the next testing period — for example, a third grader who is a 50th-percentile reader might be expected to grow 7 points from fall to winter. That number is a median; of all the third graders who are 50th percentile readers, half will grow more than 7 points, and half will grow less. If a student grows 14 points, Alpha calls this 2x growth.

The school offers students huge prizes, payouts, and incentives to perform well on those tests. That the resulting scores are higher than at other schools isn’t shocking and doesn’t say much.

But this can produce extremely odd results, particularly in high school, where term-to-term academic growth, as measured by the MAP tests, is far slower than in the early years; the expected gains for high schoolers on the MAP growth tests are close to nil as a result. For example, a ninth-grade student who is a 90th-percentile reader is expected to gain only 0.23 points on the reading MAP test from fall to spring. But this means that a ninth grader gaining two points, which is within normal random variation, would count as 9x growth!

Then, Alpha parent Peter Naimoli alleges, Alpha averages “across all students to announce a school-wide ‘2.6x Learning’ metric.” So one student growing at the expected pace and this student who gained two points would average 5x growth. Many of the reported numbers from Alpha actually have sample sizes nearly that small. The gifted and talented school, for example, was based on five kids with two test events, according to a 2025 article published in Astral Codex Ten.

If we’re admitting sample sizes that small (which we shouldn’t), I can claim that my own kids’ microschool, with four kids who showed up to both test dates and who put up some very impressive scores, also shows 3x learning. My best guess is that the gains from Alpha, or my kids’ microschool, over a conventional program are real if the program is a good fit1 — but Alpha students aren’t learning twice as much as normal students, let alone three to seven times as much.

Cold water in Arizona

One other obstacle to evaluating Alpha’s claims is the difficulty of disentangling them from selection effects: In general, the overwhelming majority of the differences between schools in student performance are driven by the self-selection of involved parents and motivated students. It stands to reason that a school serving the children of people who can afford to pay $75,000 a year is going to have better outcomes than any school that doesn’t, even if instructional quality is no better or worse.

Because Arizona’s Unbound Academy is a free public charter school based around the Alpha online platform, that particular school’s performance promises a window into the method’s effectiveness that is less distorted by selection bias.

The first year of results from Unbound, which came out earlier this month, are not encouraging on that front. Alpha had told the state of Arizona that it hoped to get 65% of the school’s students proficient in English language arts and 60% proficient in math. (The statewide averages are 42% and 34%, respectively.)

Instead, after one year, just 28% were proficient in English language arts and 10% in math.

Subscribe now

Now, that doesn’t mean that Unbound failed to teach its students anything. The student body seems to have arrived at Alpha performing well below average to begin with. If you run Alpha’s usual MAP Growth analysis, the school can report 1.8x growth.

I don’t really find it plausible that these students in any meaningful sense “learned at 1.8x” in their year at Unbound. If Alpha really had taken a bunch of incredibly low-performing students and were helping them improve, then this would be a success story — but it seems far more likely that it took a bunch of weak students who almost entirely remained weak students. They improved their standardized MAP test scores a bit more than expected because Alpha teaches to the MAP test so directly. Overall this is obviously a failure on Alpha’s own terms.

It’s not just the mitigation of selection effects that makes Unbound Academy students’ experience instructive. Unbound is a “virtual charter school” — that is, it is an online program kids log into from home. That makes it the equivalent of Alpha’s online offerings, Alpha Anywhere and GT Anywhere, not of Alpha’s on-campus programs.

Alpha Anywhere is a bundle of edtech. The promise and limitations of edtech are pretty well understood at this point (and illustrated in a just-released paper looking at Khan Academy’s AI tutor): the effect of most edtech is almost nothing; it would work OK if used as intended consistently, but almost no one uses it as intended consistently. Most students will barely use it at all if they can help it, which means it is generally not anywhere near as good as high-quality instruction from an excellent teacher or even average instruction from an average teacher.

Alpha, insofar as it has gotten results, has done so by hosting kids in an environment where they actually reliably use the edtech. That is the true magic.

It’s no surprise that Unbound Academy doesn’t appear to be getting strong results in a purely remote environment. While reporting this piece, I tested out the publicly available apps that Alpha uses as part of Timeback, and I’m broadly unimpressed with most of them. Alpha has made the baffling and ill-advised decision to use AI-generated text for most of its reading-comprehension and content-knowledge instruction.

TeachTales, one of its reading apps, churns out Harry Potter fanfiction for kids in bite-sized chunks, gated behind comprehension questions. It might increase MAP scores, but I found it deeply depressing.

Alpha’s app for arithmetic is fine but uninspiring. Getting kids to drill their arithmetic is genuinely important for higher-level math and is often a chore, so I was hopeful to hear a rumor that Alpha had something good on that front. But it’s pretty much the same as other arithmetic practice apps.2

But the regular Alpha School (the kind parents pay up to $75,000 for) isn’t just the app. It’s a campus full of activities and games and prizes — some of them extraordinarily expensive prizes (like a Nintendo Switch or an iPad) — which the students earn by finishing their work.

Subscribe now

It makes more sense to think of Alpha schools as the incentive system and environment that gets the kids to use the Timeback package properly — meaning, if there is an effective intervention, it is not Timeback itself. Just by getting kids to actually do the practice that the apps offer, Alpha seems to have made some real achievements, if not the miraculous numbers they claim.

(Alpha did not respond to my request for comment in time for publication. This piece will be updated if and when I hear back. The company has been made aware of at least some of these criticisms before: Naimoli says Alpha rejected alternative metrics he proposed, and Luke Shepard, who writes about AI learning, says he alerted the company in July 2025 to the apparent error in its white paper. Alpha has also declined to provide underlying test data to Wired and The Boston Globe. It continues to advertise 2.6x growth.)

What is school for?

To sum up, if you were imagining that “2x learning” meant something like students learning twice as much, that’s definitely not the case. And in a bunch of important ways, the students probably learn less — as far as I can determine, for instance, Alpha middle schoolers are not typically assigned any books.

But one of the most interesting things to me, as I’ve reported on Alpha School, is the program’s enduring appeal among parents who are well aware that the headline numbers are kind of meaningless.

“I love the school,” Naimoli wrote in a review that I would otherwise be inclined to call a scathing debunking of Alpha. “Alpha kids are increasing their MAP scores faster than kids at traditional schools, but the number is not 2.6 times faster. 2.6 is an erroneously computed and meaningless number.”

These sorts of testimonials put some of Alpha School’s negative press in a different light. Wired, for example, breathlessly reported on students who had a bad experience and left several years behind, dismayed by a school that set unreasonable expectations and deployed frustrating edtech. All of those things are bad. But they’re also all unfortunately and utterly normal.

It’s hard to imagine a Wired exposé of a specific local elementary school where only 20% of children learn to read. Alpha failing, in other words, is news, while the default system failing is not newsworthy at all.

This critical coverage has tended to make Alpha’s defenders double down: The system is out to get us, and everything it has to say about us could just as easily be said about any other school. But Alpha’s critics, presumably, would answer that your local public school doesn’t charge $75,000 a year, nor does it claim that it has cracked the code to revolutionizing education. And they might point out that marketing misleading growth figures is an affront to any school that is genuinely offering above-average pedagogical results, which will find itself unable to compete with Alpha’s massaged numbers.

I think the critics are right, but I think they could also do a lot to make their case more persuasive. Delivering a better criticism of Alpha School requires grappling with it on its own terms, understanding what it’s trying to do and why there’s so much excitement — and ideally articulating what the platform could do to live up to its hype.

Subscribe now

Toward that end, one of my favorite Alpha critiques is from the education writer Michael Pershan, who wrote: “I just watched like three dozen promotional videos from Alpha School. I saw young kids fencing, knitting, rock climbing, biking, jogging, petting a horse, talking to Dr. Phil, golfing, painting, training with Navy SEALs, playing piano, playing guitar, doing pullups, squatting, giving TED talks, kayaking, lighting stuff on fire, baking, running in a parking lot, and recording a podcast. But I struggled to find footage of a student reading a book.”

Alpha, he pointed out, has a very specific viewpoint on the purpose of education: They are trying to minimize time spent on core instruction while maximizing performance. This is simply not something that most schools — especially not most fancy private schools that serve the kinds of kids who can afford Alpha — are trying to do. Most schools will tell you that they are trying to build holistic thinkers and citizens or foster a love of learning. Alpha is trying to get school out of the way as fast as possible.

What to make of that depends a lot on what you expect to do with the time you save with the apps. “Get academics out of the way as fast as possible so you can focus on sports” strikes me as kind of depressing, because I don’t love youth sports, but it’s a perfectly consistent goal for those who do. Plus, we all know kids who had exactly this attitude while in a conventional school, so why not let them have it?

Much of the appeal of homeschool, too, is that you can finish work in less time and leave more time for life — for wandering barefoot in the forest, for learning to build real things with your hands, for befriending stray cats. I once saw a pitch for an Alpha School that used the freed-up time to teach kids how to build industrial civilization from scratch in the wild. I have to admit, I’d sign my kids up for that one.

But there are models I’m less interested in: The flagship Alpha campus and the San Francisco Alpha, for instance, use their post-edtech time to promote “leadership, grit, financial literacy & entrepreneurship.” If you hate this vision, then I think the right response is to articulate a competing vision.

We do have to admit that one thing that got us here was our attachment to standardized tests. I am a standardized test defender: Ultimately, standardized tests are the best tool we have to hold schools accountable for results. That is why, for all the complaints about No Child Left Behind, it got more kids proficient in math nationwide. Small improvements in test scores add up to millions of lives changed.

But while I’ll defend standardized tests, I will also acknowledge Alpha is the end stage of the testing-first mindset. “What if the only thing we care about is MAP Growth scores?” The answer is, apparently, a bunch of AI-generated comprehension questions and apps.

You can’t describe why there’s anything wrong with this unless you have a much more idealistic and comprehensive picture of what education should be.

And if you do offer a much more idealistic and comprehensive picture of what education should be — something as ambitious as rebuilding civilization from scratch, say — then you are confronted with the fact that typical schools are not achieving that either. You don’t even need as ambitious a vision as that to be disappointed all around: I condemn Alpha for not assigning real books, but that’s hardly unheard of at public middle schools either.

I hate the idea of assigning kids to read mostly AI-generated prose — but I also expect it to soon become the default, for kids and for everyone, as the whole internet drowns in a tide of AI-generated prose.

We can and should do better than Alpha. But are we doing better than Alpha?

Subscribe now

Recommended reading:

1

Naimoli lamented in a post last year, “I’ve proposed alternatives - better metrics that would actually mean something. They were rejected. Apparently “1.4 Sigma Learning” doesn’t look good on a slide deck.” He’s not the only one to make the case for 1.4: Matt Bateman, principal of Montessorium (an offshoot of Alpha), also told me he believes that “the actual statistically precise effect of Alpha on student performance is 1.4 sigma.” To be very clear, if Alpha is actually achieving 1.4 sigma learning, that would be a big deal!! I’d far rather see a carefully articulated case for 1.4 sigma gains than a sloppy case for “2x/3x learning.”

2

One notable exception to my general complaining about Alpha’s app selection is Math Academy, which I previously tried out for my oldest daughter. It is a third-party program that Alpha licenses. Math Academy is a very fast and effective program for learning the standard grade 4-12 math curriculum, but I really dislike how it teaches proofs and anything at all that’s open-ended or complicated. I think it would be pretty reasonable to use as half of a math curriculum, but I’d pair it with a lot of puzzles to teach the half of math skills it doesn’t focus on.

item.title: The public housing miracle that never happened
item.description: If you're going to build a policy agenda out of historical analogies, at least do the reading
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Worst Take of the Week is an occasional column where the author will rant about something we found stupid, annoying, bad, and/or irritating. While the title of this column was necessary for palindromic reasons, we cannot promise that entries will come out weekly or that each piece will literally be the worst take that week; this column would be boring and repetitive if each week we explained why genocide is bad in response to Twitter user @Nazi1488LoveHitler.

What if we could solve the housing crisis simply by instructing the federal government to construct beautiful fourplex apartments based on midcentury designs by Frank Lloyd Wright?

Such is the contention of Vanderbilt law professors Christopher Serkin and Daniel Sharfstein, who recently published an op-ed in The New York Times arguing that we should look to World War II-era housing policy in order to resolve the 4 million to 20 million home shortfall facing the contemporary U.S.

Current housing policy, they have argued, is afflicted with “policy myopia.” Instead of thinking big, pro-housing reformers have been excessively fixated on getting rid of the regulations that make it difficult or impossible to build housing, particularly in our highest-cost cities. They believe the federal government should step in as the authors contend it did during World War II, when it “directly built housing itself.”

Serkin and Sharfstein paint a utopian picture. Not only did the government experiment “with prefabricated construction techniques to reduce building costs and speed production” — they point to bubble houses built by spraying balloons with a concrete mixture that “went up quickly and minimized the use of scarce war material” — but it also worked with famed architects like Frank Lloyd Wright to create artistically pleasing quadplexes.

The problem with the authors’ exhortation to “remember” these lessons from the World War II housing crisis is that they are themselves refusing to learn them. Serkin and Sharfstein dwell on cherry-picked, unrepresentative examples of idyllic housing projects that were never built at scale, and they suggest that the government’s improvised construction of substandard housing for migrant workers is a model for the 21st century.

Share

What ever happened to Frank Lloyd Wright’s cloverleaf public housing project?

In both the Times op-ed and in the 71-page report the essay is based on, the authors wax poetic about a proposed “cloverleaf” project in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, designed by famed architect Frank Lloyd Wright1:

“These attached four-apartment structures were arranged in geometric patterns to create both privacy and community, with rooftop sun decks, play spaces for children, and garages tucked into the center of each building. The unusual design also allowed for shared building systems that were more efficient. From above, the cloverleaf homes looked almost organic and were an alternative to the single-family houses that private developers were primarily building,” they wrote in the op-ed.

So is it possible to visit this gorgeous paragon of publicly developed housing? No, because it doesn’t exist. According to Wright’s own account, Massachusetts architects were so annoyed at having been passed over for the project that they complained to their federal representatives. Unwilling to turn over his work to other architects, Wright then refused to sell his plans to the government and the Pittsfield project was never built.

This is not an accident of history. Indeed, the dynamic that killed the project is the very same kind of interest group protection that turbocharges NIMBYism to this day. Years later, Talbot Wegg, who was chief of the Defense Housing Division’s Planning Section, confirmed Wright’s story, recalling that then-House Majority Leader John W. McCormack took the agency to task for hiring out-of-state talent and “keeping Massachusetts architects from making a living.” A Senate hearing from 1941 reveals that the American Institute of Architects (AIA) explicitly pushed requirements that architects residing near a project should have preference over those far away. That same year, a Massachusetts Board of Housing official put it even more starkly: “New England wants local control.”

To this day, chapters of the AIA can sometimes act as NIMBY groups. AIA California opposed a bill that would have allowed eight units by right on certain lots; it opposed another that would have established a plan for 1.2 million social housing units, including 200,000 for extremely-low- and very-low-income households; and it opposed the creation of a California Housing Authority empowered to develop and acquire state-owned social housing. Local AIA chapters in Colorado, and Washington state have also opposed the removal of barriers to housing construction. These groups have also supported various pro-housing policies, my point is not to cast them all as NIMBYs but just to say that the politics of interest groups are an important barrier to overcome the U.S.’ housing supply crisis.

Not only did the cloverleaf project fail in its time — you most likely couldn’t build one today even if you wanted to. According to the National Zoning Atlas, quadplexes are legal to build on just 12% of residential land in the United States. If a developer — be it public, private, or even a nonprofit affordable housing developer — would like to take the extra time, money, and effort to ask for special permission, they are welcome to do so. They will almost certainly fail.

Subscribe now

Let’s turn to Nashville, Tennessee, where Serkin and Sharfstein both live. To my knowledge, neither Serkin nor Sharfstein made any public comment in support of Nashville’s years-long attempts to make it easier to build the multifamily housing they say they crave. In fact, in 2022, Serkin argued that there was “very, very, light zoning in Nashville” as part of an argument that regulation was not a large obstacle to addressing the area’s housing shortage — all this despite the fact that just 8% of Nashville’s residential land is zoned to permit multifamily housing.

Wright’s design also doesn’t conform to modern building codes. I took a look at Pittsfield’s existing laws as well as the building code and found the following potential violations: It’s lacking automatic sprinklers and separation between units; its stairs are too compact; its bedrooms need escape windows; its roof decks need modern guards; and its wall, window, and roof construction would not comply with energy performance needs.2 (There are probably others I don’t know about because I am not a housing developer.)

But the core thing to understand is this: Just because the government is the developer of housing doesn’t mean you can ignore the fact that local opposition, zoning restrictions, building regulations, and environmental rules exist. The government is, if anything, more restricted by these laws and the inevitable costs they impose on development, plus additional strictures like prevailing wage requirements that it imposes upon itself. (Consider, for example, New York City’s decade-long quest to build 123 affordable senior apartments on city-owned land: A neighborhood garden association sued the city under environmental regulations, and after 11 years of tribulation, the city ultimately won in 2024 but the project was ultimately abandoned due to local opposition.)

Anyone actually serious about reviving public developers would not hand-wave away the difficulties associated with overcoming localism and red tape — they would be obsessed with them.

The wrong wartime lessons

In their War Housing report, the authors paint a picture of a federal government that quickly and competently constructed almost 1 million homes: During the war, “the government built approximately 900,000 new housing units and private developers built or converted over 1,000,000.” To be clear, despite the authors’ derision of the private market, all the public housing in question required private market contractors to actually build the housing, and only in some cases did the government actually identify the sites, purchase the land, provide the financing, and manage the properties itself.3

Moreover, the vast majority of the housing built by the government was temporary shelter, unsuited to long-term use. Take the approximately 900,000 units built by the government during the war that they call evidence of “what is possible when the government gets serious about increasing housing”:

The source they are pulling from actually counts 837,000 provided or under development by the end of 1944, roughly 70% (579,700) of which were temporary. We’re talking light wood framing and plywood with communal toilets and kitchens, intentionally “below acceptable standards for permanent, peacetime dwellings.” I’m all for legalizing very cheaply made homes, but let’s not kid ourselves about whether the housing crisis could be solved with homes like these:

Wartime housing shortages were created by the rapid movement of workers into a relatively small number of industrial locations: Shipyards, ammunition plants, aircraft factories, and military installations suddenly needed tens of thousands of workers, often in places that had nowhere for those workers to live.

Where a community could permanently absorb new homes, the government looked first to privately-financed construction. Where demand was tied to a temporary war facility, the government financed housing itself and contracted with private firms to build it.

That logic explains why dormitories, trailers, communal facilities, and “demountable” homes made up a significant part of the wartime public housing program. I’m not saying these were policy failures — temporary housing is a sensible response to temporary demand — but they are just not a useful model for supplying millions of permanent homes in places where people will continue to live for decades.

The much more relevant analogy, which Serkin and Sharfstein dismiss, is what happened after the war ended.

Millions of service members returned to a country that lacked enough housing for them and their families. This was not a matter of moving a temporary workforce closer to a factory; it was a broad and durable mismatch between the number of American households and the number of American homes. That is much closer to the problem we face today.

The postwar government responded accordingly. It did not preserve the wartime emergency system of barracks and worker housing that Serkin and Sharfstein celebrate. Instead, it redirected scarce materials toward residential construction, guaranteed mortgages through the Federal Housing Administration and Veterans Administration, and encouraged builders to produce permanent homes at enormous scale. It also made infrastructure investments in energy and transportation to make it possible for the private market to meet the pressing demand for new housing.

All of the major financing tools that the federal government deployed in the postwar years to resolve the housing crisis are still available today. What’s changed? We’ve constructed an anti-growth web of political opposition, zoning regulations, environmental rules, and other restrictions that act together to choke off the private sector.

Now, on top of all that, we have to listen to law professors torture historic analogies4 and basic facts about housing policy.

The housing crisis is not about whether famous and brilliant architects can build a few dozen cool houses. It’s about whether we can quickly and efficiently build millions of homes in the places where people need them to access jobs, schools, and social networks.

Serkin and Sharfstein want you to think the private market failed to address the housing shortage, but that’s totally wrong. Enabled by government-backed financing tools — which are largely still in place today — we resolved a several-million-home shortage immediately after World War II by … helping the private market rip. By 1950, annual housing starts had reached a record 2 million, and roughly 4 million homes had been completed since the war.

It was the private market that commercialized and scaled innovations in factory-built housing, building materials, and construction methods: from mobile homes and prefabricated houses to plywood, fiberboard, and drywall, and from pre-cut wall panels to standardized plans and specialized crews moving from lot to lot in assembly-line sequence. This history is entirely missing from the one Serkin and Sharfstein tell because it’s inconvenient for their predetermined narrative.

But perhaps the biggest problem for Serkin and Sharfstein is that they remain totally ignorant of the most important problem facing a government that wants to build millions of new homes: Where are you going to get the money?

Upkeep and management of housing is not free! Managing a massive new public housing program isn’t free.

The thing about zoning is that it’s free

You know what is free? Going into your city’s zoning code, using Ctrl-F to find “minimum lot size,” and hitting delete. You can also do that for parking minimums and really anything else that has nothing to do with health and safety.

Share

What you can’t do is conjure up free money out of thin air to build a bunch of housing. The era of cheap borrowing has come to an end. If the government wants to make large capital investments or spin up brand-new programs, it will have to either raise a lot of taxes (in the middle of a de facto tax revolt) or else borrow even more money, putting existing programs like Medicare or Social Security at risk.

An April 2025 report about the cost of housing shows that publicly financed affordable housing cost 1.5 times the average cost of market rate housing in California and more than four times the cost market-rate housing in Texas.5

This is a big reason why upzoning is so attractive. Taxpayers don’t have to pay out of pocket for an untested massive public housing program and can instead count on a bunch of private individuals, banks, and corporations to try to build a variety of new homes that will suddenly be legal if we upzone. Having private actors take on this risk themselves is actually better than expecting the government to build anywhere from 4 million to 20 million new homes. That’s not a worst-case scenario; that’s a best-case scenario.

Serkin and Sharfstein seem completely unaware of — or perhaps merely uninterested in — the boring details of land acquisition, available public financing tools, or the struggles the government has faced in management and upkeep of its existing public housing stock. None of these problems are meaningfully discussed in either their op-ed or their 71-page report.

The authors claim that they are merely annoyed by the overfocus on zoning, but previous scholarship indicates that their animosity toward removing existing barriers to housing is more pronounced than they admit.

Back in 2020, before the left had largely accepted the YIMBY diagnosis of the housing crisis, Serkin penned an article in the Notre Dame Law Review called “A Case for Zoning.” In it, he offers a “defense of zoning, and in particular density regulations.” Serkin argues that by “maintaining community character, enhancing property values, and allocating the costs of development between insiders and outsiders,” zoning offers a critical defense for incumbent homeowners.

It’s important to realize when someone is offering a good faith critique versus when they’ve exhibited longstanding hostility to the project of solving the housing supply crisis.

“Perhaps needless to say, these uses of zoning can easily shade into NIMBYism … and naked exclusion,” Serkin concedes before plowing forward, undeterred. He later adds, “A new apartment building in the middle of Manhattan is more consistent with reasonable expectations than the same building in Nashville, Tennessee.”

I’m sure Serkin’s concern for his neighbors in Nashville is entirely selfless.

Subscribe now

Update 8/26/2026: This piece has been updated to further explain the policy positions of modern local AIA chapters.

Previous WTOTW:

1

The Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator, which published the War Housing report written by Serkin and Sharfstein, was created to “conduct foundational research and work through the nuts and bolts of policy implementation.” If this report is what counts for nuts and bolts, we are in trouble. Unsurprisingly, the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator was funded in no small part by $1.5 million from the Hewlett Foundation’s Economy and Society project, which seems to largely exist to spread economic misinformation.

2

Wright's available plans are not complete, so it's possible that some of these would have been addressed.

3

It’s normal to refer to the government as “building” infrastructure even if it contracts private firms to do the actual construction but in a piece where they are drawing such sharp distinctions between public and private development, deriding the latter, and failing to make clear the private markets role in public development, the use of the phrase “build” is misleading. They seem to even confuse themselves. At one point they claim that the Division of Defense Housing Coordination “recommended building 1,000 housing units and financing an additional 10,000 privately built units.” But their cited source says the paln called for “1,000 government-financed and 10,000 privately built family units.” Their paraphrase thus converts the government-financed units into government-built units while appearing to attribute government financing to the 10,000 privately built units. In a sufficiently capacious sense, much privately built housing is publicly financed. But if federally financed private construction counts as government building, then the postwar FHA/VA boom they dismiss as a failure is the largest public housing program in American history.

4

My editor made me cut this, but one of the most absurd anecdotes they linger on is the “bubble house” experiment in Falls Church, Virginia, where the government tested an “experimental system of spraying concrete onto hemispherical balloon forms” that would conserve materials necessary for the war effort by using neither wood nor metal. We’re talking about 12 houses that ultimately suffered from “moisture problems, crumbling plaster, and the difficulty of decorating curved walls.”

5

The main causes were that affordable housing developers had to “pay substantially above-market wages and unusually large architectural and engineering fees (particularly in Los Angeles) likely related to highly prescriptive design requirements.”

item.title: How do I listen to The Argument podcast without ads in my podcast app?
item.description: Go to The Argument podcast tab at the top of theargumentmag.com or visit theargumentmag.com/s/the-argument-podcast. Click RSS Feed (or “more” if you don’t see it) to copy the feed link, then paste it into your podcast app:
item.content:encoded:
By The Argument

Go to The Argument podcast tab at the top of theargumentmag.com or visit theargumentmag.com/s/the-argument-podcast. Click RSS Feed (or “more” if you don’t see it) to copy the feed link, then paste it into your podcast app:

  • Apple Podcasts: On The Argument podcast webpage, click the Apple Podcasts tab, then paste the link into the “Podcast URL” bar.

  • Overcast: Click the plus sign, select Add URL, and paste the link.

  • Pocket Casts: Paste the link into the search bar. When the show appears, tap the plus sign to add it.

Tip: In most podcast apps, you can paste the URL into the search bar or an “Add URL” option.

For more help, see Substack’s guide to listening in a podcast app.

Happy listening!
